topics.title: Overview, Objectives & Key Definitions
topics.concept:
Unit Overview

This unit uses the first and second derivatives to describe the shape of a graph: where it rises and falls, where it peaks and dips, and how it bends. These tools let you locate extrema, identify concavity and inflection points, and solve optimization problems ("find the maximum/minimum"). It also formalizes the key existence theorems — the Mean Value Theorem (MVT) and Extreme Value Theorem (EVT).

This is the largest analytic unit (14 topics) and a major exam contributor, especially on free-response, where justification using derivative signs is essential.

Big picture: f' controls increasing/decreasing and extrema; f'' controls concavity and inflection.

Learning Objectives

  • State and apply the Mean Value Theorem and Extreme Value Theorem.
  • Use f' to find intervals of increase/decrease and local extrema (First Derivative Test).
  • Use f'' to determine concavity and inflection points, and apply the Second Derivative Test.
  • Find absolute extrema on a closed interval (candidates test).
  • Interpret relationships among the graphs of f, f', f''.
  • Solve optimization problems.
  • Analyze implicitly defined curves (tangents, extrema).

Prerequisite Concepts

  • Fluent differentiation (Units 2–3) and critical-point solving.
  • Sign analysis (number lines / sign charts).
  • The theorems of Unit 1 (IVT) and continuity/differentiability.

Key Definitions

  • Critical number: a value c where f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) is undefined (and f is defined at c).
  • Local (relative) maximum/minimum: highest/lowest value in a neighborhood.
  • Absolute (global) extremum: highest/lowest value over the entire domain/interval.
  • Concave up: f'' > 0 (slopes increasing, graph opens upward); concave down: f'' < 0.
  • Inflection point: a point where concavity changes (f'' changes sign).

quiz.q: The Mean Value Theorem requires that a function f be:
options: continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b)
quiz.explanation: The MVT hypotheses are: f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] and differentiable on the open interval (a, b).

quiz.q: The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that a function attains an absolute maximum and minimum if it is:
options: continuous on a closed interval [a, b]
quiz.explanation: The EVT states that a function continuous on a closed, bounded interval [a, b] attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on that interval.

quiz.q: A function f is increasing on an interval when:
quiz.explanation: A positive first derivative means the function is increasing on that interval.

quiz.q: A critical number of f is a value where:
quiz.explanation: Critical numbers occur where the first derivative equals zero or does not exist (and f is defined).

quiz.q: By the Second Derivative Test, if f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, then f has a:
quiz.explanation: A positive second derivative at a critical point indicates the function is concave up there, giving a local minimum.

topics.title: Important Theorems & Formulas
topics.concept:
Important Theorems

Extreme Value Theorem (EVT): A function continuous on a closed interval [a, b] attains an absolute max and an absolute min on [a, b].

Mean Value Theorem (MVT): If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there exists c in (a, b) with f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a) (a tangent parallel to the secant). Rolle's Theorem is the case f(a) = f(b), giving f'(c) = 0.

First Derivative Test: At a critical number c, if f' changes + to −, local max; − to +, local min; no sign change, neither.

Second Derivative Test: At a critical number c with f'(c) = 0: if f''(c) > 0, local min; if f''(c) < 0, local max; if f''(c) = 0, inconclusive (use the First Derivative Test).

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^2 on [1, 3], find the value c guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem.
quiz.explanation: The average rate of change is (f(3) - f(1))/(3 - 1) = (9 - 1)/2 = 4. Set f'(c) = 2c = 4, so c = 2.

quiz.q: The Mean Value Theorem guarantees a point where the tangent line is parallel to:
options: the secant line through the endpoints
quiz.explanation: The MVT guarantees a c where the instantaneous rate f'(c) equals the average rate, so the tangent line at c is parallel to the secant line joining the endpoints.

quiz.q: Rolle's Theorem is a special case of the MVT that applies when:
quiz.explanation: When f(a) = f(b), the average rate of change is 0, so Rolle's Theorem guarantees a c with f'(c) = 0.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^2 - 2x on [0, 4], the value c from the MVT is:
Which situation could prevent the Extreme Value Theorem from guaranteeing an absolute maximum?
options: The interval is open, such as (0, 1)
quiz.explanation: The EVT requires a closed interval. On an open interval, a continuous function may fail to attain an absolute maximum or minimum.

topics.title: Concept Explanations & Solved Examples
topics.concept:
Concept Explanations

Increasing/decreasing and extrema (5.3–5.4). Build a sign chart of f' using critical numbers. f rises where f' > 0, falls where f' < 0; sign changes locate local extrema.

Concavity and inflection (5.8, 5.10). A sign chart of f'' shows concavity. An inflection point requires f'' to change sign — a zero of f'' alone is not enough (e.g., x⁴ at 0).

Reading f, f', f'' together (5.9). These are the highest-value skills:

  • f increasing ⇔ f' > 0; f has local max where f' changes + → −.
  • f concave up ⇔ f'' > 0 ⇔ f' increasing.
  • A local min of f' corresponds to an inflection point of f.

Absolute extrema (5.5). On a closed interval, the max/min is always among the critical values and the endpoints — just compare the candidate values.

Optimization (5.12). The art is translating words into an objective function of one variable. Classic results: for fixed perimeter the max-area rectangle is a square; for a fixed-volume closed cylinder, minimum surface area occurs when height = diameter.

MVT applications (5.6). MVT connects average and instantaneous rates: if a car averages 60 mph, at some instant its speedometer read exactly 60. It also proves that f' = 0 everywhere ⇒ f is constant, and bounds like f'(x) ≤ 2 ⇒ f(b) − f(a) ≤ 2(b − a).

Worked Examples

Example 1 (First Derivative Test). For f(x) = x³ − 3x, f'(x) = 3(x−1)(x+1). f' changes + → − at x = −1 (local max) and − → + at x = 1 (local min).

Example 2 (Second Derivative Test). Same f: f''(x) = 6x. f''(1) = 6 > 0 ⇒ local min at x = 1; f''(−1) = −6 < 0 ⇒ local max at x = −1.

Example 3 (Absolute extrema). f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 2]: critical x = 1. f(0) = 0, f(1) = −2, f(2) = 2. Absolute max 2 (x = 2), absolute min −2 (x = 1).

Example 4 (Inflection). f(x) = x³ − 6x²: f''(x) = 6x − 12 = 0 at x = 2, and f'' changes sign there — inflection point at x = 2.

Example 5 (Optimization). Two nonnegative numbers sum to 12; maximize the product. P = x(12 − x), P'(x) = 12 − 2x = 0 at x = 6, product = 36.

Example 6 (MVT). For f(x) = x² on [1, 3]: average rate = (9 − 1)/2 = 4; set 2c = 4 ⇒ c = 2.

quiz.q: According to the EVT, the absolute extrema of a continuous function on [a, b] must occur at:
quiz.explanation: Absolute extrema on a closed interval occur either at interior critical points (where f' = 0 or is undefined) or at the endpoints.

quiz.q: On what interval is f(x) = x^2 - 4x increasing?
quiz.explanation: f'(x) = 2x - 4 > 0 when x > 2, so f is increasing for x > 2.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x, on what interval is f decreasing?
quiz.explanation: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1) < 0 for -1 < x < 1, so f is decreasing there.

quiz.q: If f'(x) = (x - 2)(x + 3), on what interval is f decreasing?
quiz.explanation: f'(x) < 0 between the roots -3 and 2, so f is decreasing on -3 < x < 2.

quiz.q: For f(x) = e^x - x, on what interval is f increasing?
quiz.explanation: f'(x) = e^x - 1 > 0 when e^x > 1, i.e., when x > 0.

topics.title: Graphical Interpretation, Common Mistakes & Tips
topics.concept:
Graphical Interpretation

  • f' graph: above the axis ⇒ f increasing; zeros with sign change ⇒ f's local extrema; f' increasing ⇒ f concave up.
  • f'' graph: sign gives concavity; sign changes give inflection points of f.
  • A smooth "peak" of f sits above a downward zero-crossing of f'; a "valley" above an upward crossing.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling every zero of f'' an inflection point — the sign must change.
  • Reporting a critical number as the answer instead of the max/min value (or point).
  • Skipping endpoints in a closed-interval absolute-extrema problem.
  • Trusting the Second Derivative Test when f''(c) = 0 — it's inconclusive; use the First Derivative Test.
  • Weak justification on free-response — you must cite the sign behavior of f' or f''.
  • Ignoring MVT/EVT hypotheses (continuity/differentiability) when the theorem is invoked.

AP Exam Tips

  • On free-response, justify with a sign chart or explicit sign statement ("f' changes from positive to negative, so f has a local max").
  • Absolute extrema on [a, b]: always run the candidates test (criticals + endpoints).
  • For "f is increasing/concave up on…", answer with intervals and the derivative reasoning.
  • Know the classic optimization results to sanity-check answers.
  • State the hypotheses when citing MVT or EVT — it earns the justification point.

Unit Summary

  • f' : increasing/decreasing and local extrema (First Derivative Test).
  • f'' : concavity and inflection points (Second Derivative Test, when f''(c) ≠ 0).
  • Absolute extrema on [a, b] come from the candidates test (criticals + endpoints).
  • MVT: f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a); EVT: continuous on closed interval ⇒ attains max and min.
  • Optimization: reduce to one variable, then use critical-point analysis.

Next unit: the reverse process — integration and accumulation of change.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 on [0, 2], find the value c from the Mean Value Theorem.
quiz.explanation: Average rate = (8 - 0)/2 = 4. f'(c) = 3c^2 = 4, so c^2 = 4/3 and c = 2/sqrt(3) (taking the value in (0, 2)).

quiz.q: Why does f(x) = 1/x fail to have an absolute maximum on (0, 1]?
options: f is not continuous on a closed interval containing 0 and grows without bound as x approaches 0
quiz.explanation: As x approaches 0 from the right, 1/x approaches infinity. The interval is not closed at 0, so the EVT does not apply and no absolute maximum exists.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x, on what interval(s) is f increasing?
For f(x) = x + 1/x (x > 0), at what x is there a local minimum?
quiz.explanation: f'(x) = 1 - 1/x^2 = 0 gives x^2 = 1, so x = 1 (for x > 0). f' changes from negative to positive there, a local minimum.

quiz.q: Find the absolute maximum of f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [0, 2].

mock_tests.title: Practice Set A

questions.q: A function is concave up on an interval when:
questions.explanation: A positive second derivative means the function is concave up (its slope is increasing).

questions.q: An inflection point of f occurs where:
questions.explanation: An inflection point is where the graph changes concavity, which requires f'' to change sign.

questions.q: If f'(x) < 0 on an interval, then on that interval f is:
questions.explanation: A negative first derivative means the function is decreasing.

questions.q: At a local extremum of a differentiable function, the first derivative is:
questions.explanation: For a differentiable function, local extrema occur where f'(x) = 0.

questions.q: The conclusion of the Mean Value Theorem is that there exists c in (a, b) such that:
questions.explanation: The MVT concludes that some interior point c has instantaneous rate f'(c) equal to the average rate of change over [a, b].

questions.q: An absolute extremum on a closed interval is:
options: the single largest (or smallest) function value on the whole interval
questions.explanation: An absolute (global) extremum is the largest or smallest value the function attains over the entire interval.

questions.q: By the First Derivative Test, f has a local maximum at c if f' changes from:
questions.explanation: A local maximum occurs where the function stops increasing and starts decreasing, i.e., f' changes from positive to negative.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x, at which x is there a local maximum?
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 3(x-1)(x+1). At x = -1, f' changes from positive (x < -1) to negative (-1 < x < 1), a local maximum.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x, at which x is there a local minimum?
questions.explanation: At x = 1, f' changes from negative to positive, indicating a local minimum.

questions.q: How many critical numbers does f(x) = x^4 - 4x^2 have?
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 8x = 4x(x^2 - 2) = 0 gives x = 0, x = sqrt(2), x = -sqrt(2): three critical numbers.

questions.q: If f'(x) = x^2 (does not change sign at x = 0), what happens at x = 0?
options: There is no local extremum (f' does not change sign)
questions.explanation: Although x = 0 is a critical number, f'(x) = x^2 >= 0 on both sides, so f' does not change sign and there is no local extremum.

questions.q: Find the absolute maximum of f(x) = x^2 on the interval [-1, 3].
questions.explanation: Candidates: critical point x = 0 (f = 0) and endpoints x = -1 (f = 1), x = 3 (f = 9). The absolute maximum is 9.

questions.q: Find the absolute minimum of f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1 on [0, 3].
The 'candidates test' for absolute extrema on [a, b] evaluates f at:
options: all critical points in [a, b] and both endpoints
questions.explanation: To find absolute extrema on a closed interval, compare f-values at every critical point and at both endpoints.

questions.q: If f'(x) = 0 for all x in an interval, then on that interval f is:
questions.explanation: A consequence of the MVT: if the derivative is zero everywhere on an interval, the function is constant there.

questions.q: If two functions f and g satisfy f'(x) = g'(x) for all x, then:
options: f(x) = g(x) + C for some constant C
questions.explanation: If two functions have equal derivatives on an interval, they differ by a constant: f(x) - g(x) = C.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x, use the Second Derivative Test at x = 1.
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 6x, so f''(1) = 6 > 0. The function is concave up at x = 1, giving a local minimum.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x, apply the Second Derivative Test at x = -1.
questions.explanation: f''(-1) = 6(-1) = -6 < 0. The function is concave down, giving a local maximum.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^2 + 4x, the Second Derivative Test at the critical point x = -2 shows:
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 2x + 4 = 0 at x = -2. f''(x) = 2 > 0, so x = -2 is a local minimum.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^3, on what interval is f concave down?
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 6x < 0 when x < 0, so f is concave down for x < 0.

mock_tests.title: Practice Set B

questions.q: For f(x) = x^4, describe the concavity.
options: Concave up for all x (except possibly x = 0)
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 12x^2 >= 0, and is positive for all x not equal to 0, so f is concave up.

questions.q: Concave up means the graph:
options: opens upward and lies above its tangent lines
questions.explanation: A concave-up curve bends upward (like a cup) and lies above each of its tangent lines.

questions.q: If f'(x) > 0 and f''(x) < 0 on an interval, the graph of f is:
questions.explanation: f' > 0 means increasing; f'' < 0 means concave down. So the graph rises while bending downward.

questions.q: If the graph of f' is increasing on an interval, then f is:
questions.explanation: f' increasing means f'' > 0, which means f is concave up.

questions.q: If f'(c) = 0 and f' changes from negative to positive at c, then the graph of f has:
questions.explanation: f' going from negative to positive means f goes from decreasing to increasing: a local minimum.

questions.q: Find the inflection point of f(x) = x^3.
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 6x = 0 at x = 0, and f'' changes sign there (negative to positive), so x = 0 is an inflection point.

questions.q: For f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 5, at what x is the inflection point?
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 6x - 12 = 0 at x = 2, and concavity changes there, so x = 2 is an inflection point.

questions.q: The number of inflection points of f(x) = x^4 - 6x^2 is:
questions.explanation: f''(x) = 12x^2 - 12 = 12(x^2 - 1) = 0 at x = 1 and x = -1, with sign changes at both, giving 2 inflection points.

questions.q: The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a solution to f(x) = k on [a, b] if f is continuous and:
options: k is between f(a) and f(b)
questions.explanation: The IVT guarantees that a continuous function takes every value k between f(a) and f(b) at some point in [a, b].

questions.q: Which theorem guarantees a continuous function on [a, b] attains its maximum value?
questions.explanation: The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that a function continuous on a closed interval attains an absolute maximum (and minimum).

questions.q: A rectangle has a fixed perimeter of 40. What dimensions maximize its area?
questions.explanation: With perimeter 40, l + w = 20. Area A = w(20 - w) is maximized at w = 10, giving a 10 by 10 square with area 100.

questions.q: What is the minimum value of the sum S = x + 16/x for x > 0?
questions.explanation: S'(x) = 1 - 16/x^2 = 0 at x = 4. S(4) = 4 + 4 = 8, a minimum since S'' > 0.

questions.q: The first step in solving an optimization problem is usually to:
options: write the quantity to optimize as a function of one variable
questions.explanation: You express the objective (e.g., area or cost) as a function of a single variable using the constraint, then find critical points.

questions.q: The difference between an absolute maximum and a relative (local) maximum is:
options: an absolute maximum is the highest value on the whole domain; a relative maximum is highest only nearby
a relative maximum is always higher
an absolute maximum occurs only at endpoints
questions.explanation: An absolute (global) maximum is the largest value over the entire domain, while a relative (local) maximum is the largest value only in a neighborhood.

questions.q: A relative extremum of a differentiable function can only occur where:
questions.explanation: For a differentiable function, relative extrema occur only at critical points where f'(x) = 0 (Fermat's Theorem).

questions.q: If f'(x) = -2x + 6, on what interval is f increasing?
questions.explanation: f'(x) = -2x + 6 > 0 when x < 3, so f is increasing for x < 3.

questions.q: For f(x) = 3x^4 - 4x^3, the critical numbers are:
For f(x) = -x^2 + 6x, describe the concavity everywhere.
questions.explanation: f''(x) = -2 < 0 for all x, so the parabola is concave down everywhere.

questions.q: Find the absolute maximum of f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x on [-2, 3].
A function continuous on [2, 8] is guaranteed by the EVT to have:
options: both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [2, 8]
questions.explanation: The EVT guarantees that a function continuous on a closed, bounded interval attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.
